sources.citation: Eime, R. M., Young, J. A., Harvey, J. T., Charity, M. J., & Payne, W. R. (2013). A systematic review of the psychological and social benefits of participation in sport for children and adolescents. International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity.
sources.finding: A review of 30 studies found sport participation associated with higher self-esteem, better social interaction and fewer depressive symptoms, with team sport associated with better outcomes than individual activities.
sources.limits: 21 of the 30 studies were cross-sectional, so the direction of cause is unclear.

sources.citation: Visek, A. J., Achrati, S. M., Mannix, H., McDonnell, K., Harris, B. S., & DiPietro, L. (2015). The fun integration theory: Toward sustaining children and adolescents sport participation. Journal of Physical Activity and Health.
sources.finding: Concept mapping with 142 youth soccer players, 37 coaches and 57 parents produced 81 things that make sport fun, grouped into 11 dimensions such as trying hard, positive coaching and learning and improving.
sources.limits: Older children. That winning ranked low is from prior knowledge, not the abstract read.

sources.citation: Carson, V., Lee, E.-Y., Hewitt, L., Jennings, C., Hunter, S., Kuzik, N., et al. (2017). Systematic review of the relationships between physical activity and health indicators in the early years (0-4 years). BMC Public Health.
sources.finding: Physical activity in children up to age 4 was favourably associated with motor development, fitness, bone health and cardiometabolic health, with weaker evidence for cognitive development.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Basis of guideline `who-2019`.

sources.citation: Sandseter, E. B. H., & Kennair, L. E. O. (2011). Children's risky play from an evolutionary perspective: The anti-phobic effects of thrilling experiences. Evolutionary Psychology.
sources.finding: Proposed that thrilling play with heights, speed and rough-and-tumble exposes children to fears in manageable doses and may protect against later anxiety.
sources.limits: A theoretical argument, not a test.

sources.citation: Jayanthi, N. A., LaBella, C. R., Fischer, D., Pasulka, J., & Dugas, L. R. (2015). Sports-specialized intensive training and the risk of injury in young athletes: A clinical case-control study. American Journal of Sports Medicine.
sources.finding: Among 1,190 athletes aged 7-18, highly specialised athletes, and those training more hours a week than their age in years, had higher odds of serious overuse injuries.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Older children.

sources.citation: Obradović, J., Sulik, M. J., & Shaffer, A. (2021). Learning to let go: Parental over-engagement predicts poorer self-regulation in kindergartners. Journal of Family Psychology.
sources.finding: In videotaped play with about 100 kindergartners, parents who kept directing, teaching or correcting while the child was already engaged had children with poorer self-regulation in tasks and in teacher reports.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Correlational.

sources.citation: Perry, N. B., Dollar, J. M., Calkins, S. D., Keane, S. P., & Shanahan, L. (2018). Childhood self-regulation as a mechanism through which early overcontrolling parenting is associated with adjustment in preadolescence. Developmental Psychology.
sources.finding: In 422 children assessed at 2, 5 and 10, overcontrolling parenting at age 2 was associated with poorer emotion and behaviour regulation at 5, and better regulation at 5 with fewer emotional problems and better school and social outcomes at 10.
sources.limits: Read from a press release. Correlational.

sources.citation: Rapee, R. M., Kennedy, S., Ingram, M., Edwards, S., & Sweeney, L. (2005). Prevention and early intervention of anxiety disorders in inhibited preschool children. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology.
sources.finding: In 146 very shy preschoolers, six parent group sessions on reducing overprotection and encouraging gradual exposure led to fewer anxiety diagnoses a year later than no intervention.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Children selected for high inhibition.

sources.citation: Lebowitz, E. R., Marin, C., Martino, A., Shimshoni, Y., & Silverman, W. K. (2020). Parent-based treatment as efficacious as cognitive-behavioral therapy for childhood anxiety: A randomized noninferiority study of Supportive Parenting for Anxious Childhood Emotions. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry.
sources.finding: In 124 children aged 7-14 with an anxiety disorder, 12 weekly sessions of a parent-only program that taught parents to reduce accommodation of the child's anxiety and express confidence in the child reduced anxiety as much as CBT delivered to the child.
sources.limits: Read from an NIH summary; published online in 2019. Clinical sample, older children.

sources.citation: Mueller, C. M., & Dweck, C. S. (1998). Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
sources.finding: In six studies, starting with 128 fifth graders, children praised for intelligence after a success persisted less, enjoyed the task less and performed worse after a later failure than children praised for effort.
sources.limits: Older children. See `li-bates-2019` for failed replications.

sources.citation: Li, Y., & Bates, T. C. (2019). You can't change your basic ability, but you work at things, and that's how we get hard things done: Testing the role of growth mindset on response to setbacks, educational attainment, and cognitive ability. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General.
sources.finding: In three studies with more than 600 children aged 9-13 in China and the UK, a growth-mindset manipulation did not improve resilience after failure, and mindset was not related to grades.
sources.limits: Read from a university news release.

sources.citation: Brummelman, E., Thomaes, S., Orobio de Castro, B., Overbeek, G., & Bushman, B. J. (2014). "That's not just beautiful - that's incredibly beautiful!": The adverse impact of inflated praise on children with low self-esteem. Psychological Science.
sources.finding: Adults gave inflated praise about twice as often to children with low self-esteem. In an experiment with 240 children, children with low self-esteem who were told a drawing was 'incredibly beautiful' then chose easier drawings to copy; children with high self-esteem chose harder ones.
sources.limits: Read from a press release. Older children.

sources.citation: Havighurst, S. S., Wilson, K. R., Harley, A. E., Prior, M. R., & Kehoe, C. (2010). Tuning in to Kids: Improving emotion socialization practices in parents of preschool children - findings from a community trial. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry.
sources.finding: Parents of preschoolers randomised to a six-session emotion-coaching program became less dismissive and more coaching of emotions, and their children's behaviour problems fell more than in the control group.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Parent and teacher reports.

sources.citation: Leonard, J. A., Lee, Y., & Schulz, L. E. (2017). Infants make more attempts to achieve a goal when they see adults persist. Science.
sources.finding: Fifteen-month-olds who watched an adult try hard and succeed at two tasks tried harder on a new toy than infants who watched the adult succeed easily.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Infants, one lab session.

sources.citation: Gray, P., Lancy, D. F., & Bjorklund, D. F. (2023). Decline in independent activity as a cause of decline in children's mental well-being: Summary of the evidence. Journal of Pediatrics.
sources.finding: Argues that the decline over decades in children's opportunity to play, roam and act without adult supervision is a cause of rising anxiety and depression.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. An argument from trends and correlations by advocates of the position.

sources.citation: Durlak, J. A., Weissberg, R. P., Dymnicki, A. B., Taylor, R. D., & Schellinger, K. B. (2011). The impact of enhancing students' social and emotional learning: A meta-analysis of school-based universal interventions. Child Development.
sources.finding: Across 213 school programs for about 270,000 students from kindergarten to high school, social and emotional learning programs improved social-emotional skills, attitudes and behaviour, and academic performance by about 11 percentile points.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Later work suggests smaller effects in independent evaluations.

sources.citation: Murano, D., Sawyer, J. E., & Lipnevich, A. A. (2020). A meta-analytic review of preschool social and emotional learning interventions. Review of Educational Research.
sources.finding: Preschool social and emotional learning programs improved children's social-emotional competence and reduced problem behaviour.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Classroom programs.

sources.citation: Jirout, J. J., & Newcombe, N. S. (2015). Building blocks for developing spatial skills: Evidence from a large, representative U.S. sample. Psychological Science.
sources.finding: In 847 children aged 4-7, those who played with puzzles, blocks or board games more than six times a week scored higher on a block-design spatial test than those who played less, alongside effects of family income and general ability.
sources.limits: Read from a journal-society news article. Correlational.

sources.citation: Fisher, K. R., Hirsh-Pasek, K., Newcombe, N., & Golinkoff, R. M. (2013). Taking shape: Supporting preschoolers' acquisition of geometric knowledge through guided play. Child Development.
sources.finding: 60 children aged 4 and 5 (mean 56 months) learned about four shapes by guided play, direct instruction or free play. The guided-play group was best at recognising atypical shapes as real triangles, rectangles and so on, and the gain held a week later.
sources.limits: Mostly white, upper-middle-class sample; four shapes only.

sources.citation: Casey, B. M., Andrews, N., Schindler, H., Kersh, J. E., Samper, A., & Copley, J. (2008). The development of spatial skills through interventions involving block building activities. Cognition and Instruction.
sources.finding: The What Works Clearinghouse rated this kindergarten block-building trial as meeting its standards without reservations. Children who built increasingly complex structures, especially within a story, improved on spatial tasks.
sources.limits: Results from prior knowledge; the clearinghouse page read did not show effect sizes. Classroom program.

sources.citation: Wai, J., Lubinski, D., & Benbow, C. P. (2009). Spatial ability for STEM domains: Aligning over 50 years of cumulative psychological knowledge solidifies its importance. Journal of Educational Psychology.
sources.finding: In a US sample of about 400,000 high school students followed for 11 years, spatial ability predicted earning STEM degrees and working in STEM beyond what verbal and math ability predicted.
sources.limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Adolescent ability; says nothing about training it early.

sources.citation: Wolfgang, C. H., Stannard, L. L., & Jones, I. (2001). Block play performance among preschoolers as a predictor of later school achievement in mathematics. Journal of Research in Childhood Education.
sources.finding: In 37 children followed from age 4, the complexity of preschool block building did not predict math at grades 3 or 5, but did predict standardised math scores at grade 7 and high-school math course-taking, controlling for IQ, gender and family income.
sources.limits: Very small single-preschool sample; the authors say causation was not established.

sources.citation: de Bruin, A., Treccani, B., & Della Sala, S. (2015). Cognitive advantage in bilingualism: An example of publication bias? Psychological Science.
sources.finding: Of 104 conference abstracts on bilingualism and executive control, 63% of those supporting a bilingual advantage were later published in journals, against 36% of those that did not support it.
sources.limits: Read from the journal society's press release.

sources.citation: Hoff, E., Core, C., Place, S., Rumiche, R., Señor, M., & Parra, M. (2012). Dual language exposure and early bilingual development. Journal of Child Language.
sources.finding: Comparing high-income bilingual and monolingual children aged 1 year 10 months to 2 years 6 months, monolinguals were ahead on vocabulary and grammar in their one language, but the groups were comparable in total vocabulary across languages.
sources.limits: Toddlers.

sources.citation: Ferjan Ramírez, N., & Kuhl, P. (2017). Bilingual baby: Foreign language intervention in Madrid's infant education centers. Mind, Brain, and Education.
sources.finding: 280 children aged 7 to 33 months in Madrid centres received 18 weeks of daily English play sessions with tutors. They produced about 74 English words or phrases per child per hour against 13 in the comparison group, and kept the gain 18 weeks later.
sources.limits: Read from a university press release. Very young children with intensive live exposure.

sources.citation: Jaekel, N., Schurig, M., Florian, M., & Ritter, M. (2017). From early starters to late finishers? A longitudinal study of early foreign language learning in school. Language Learning.
sources.finding: Among 5,130 students in 31 academic-track German schools, those who began English in grade 1 were ahead in reading and listening in grade 5, but by grade 7 those who began in grade 3 were ahead.
sources.limits: Read from a university press release. Early lessons were at most 90 minutes a week.
